headline: Product designer confirms new smartphone 'innovation' is just a physical hole in the chassis to store loose fennel seeds
body:
Q: The new iPhone 18 Pro has everyone talking about its return to 'vintage' engineering. Can you walk us through the design philosophy behind that circular cavity on the bottom left side?

A: Absolutely. We noticed that while our users were paying for state-of-the-art processors, they were constantly struggling with the post-meal etiquette of fresh breath. We decided to bridge the gap between high-end computational power and traditional digestive aid by providing a dedicated, recessed storage chamber for mukhwas.

Q: It’s being marketed as an 'Analog Refresh Port.' Isn't that just a fancy way of saying you’ve brought back a feature most tech companies killed off a decade ago?

A: We prefer to view it as 'Hyper-Local Ergonomics.' Unlike Android flagships that prioritized slimness at the cost of your post-Biryani experience, our design team spent six months researching the optimal volume required to hold exactly two pinches of saunf without the seeds interfering with the haptic engine.

Q: Is there any risk of the seeds causing hardware failure if they migrate into the charging port?

A: We’ve integrated a proprietary 'Scent-Seal' technology. It ensures the refreshing aroma of fennel persists even when the battery is at one percent, and the internal sensors are calibrated to differentiate between a structural hardware glitch and a stray piece of sugar-coated candy. It’s about merging the digital and the flavorful.
caption: The future is here, and it smells like a digestive aid. We caught up with the design lead on the latest flagship release to discuss why they decided to prioritize post-meal freshness. #Smartphone #Innovation #TechNews #Fennel (satire)
